scenarios.title: Scenario 4 — Developer Productivity with Claude
scenarios.brief: A language-learning company's platform team uses Claude Code on a large Ruby on Rails app with a React front end. Engineers read and change code with the built-in tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep and Glob. MCP servers connect Claude to Linear and a staging Postgres database. Some engineers also script Claude with the Agent SDK for internal tools.

questions.question: Errors spiked after Tuesday's deploy, and the stack trace ends in one method, apply_regional_discount. The engineer needs every path in the app that calls it. In this same session they will then write the fix, with the callers' real code in front of Claude. The session is fresh, and billing code is spread across many folders. How should Claude trace the callers?

options.t: Glob for files with price or billing in their names, then Read the ones that look relevant.
options.why: Works, but only usually. File names hint at content, but callers in jobs, controllers or views with other names are missed.

options.t: Read every file in the billing folders in turn, noting a short summary of each in a scratchpad file.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. It finds the callers, but it fills the context with files that don't matter before any tracing starts.

options.t: Ask an Explore subagent to map the call paths, and work from the short summary it returns.
options.why: Works, but the code stays in the subagent. The summary lists paths, but the engineer wants the callers' real code in this session for the fix.

options.t: Grep for the method's name, Read each match, then trace each caller outward one step at a time.
options.why: Best. Grep finds every call by content, Read brings the real code into this session, and each step out follows what the last read showed.

questions.decider: In this same session they will then write the fix, with the callers' real code in front of Claude.
questions.explanation: Build understanding incrementally: Grep for references, Read the hits, follow the trail outward. An Explore subagent suits verbose discovery when only a summary is needed, not when the code itself must be in the main session.

eli5.question: Claude must find every place that calls one method, and later fix it with that code in view. The clue: with the callers' real code in front of Claude. It is not about speed.
eli5.answer: Think of tracing a family tree. You start with one person, find their parents, then their parents' parents, one step at a time. You don't read the whole town register first. In code that means Grep for the method's name (search inside files), Read each hit, then step outward. Everything you read stays in your session, ready for the fix. Rule: trace from a known point with Grep, then Read outward step by step.
options: Picking files by their names is judging a book by its cover. Callers with other names get missed.
Reading the whole town register finds everyone, but it floods your desk with strangers first.
A helper's summary would win if a list were enough. Here the real code must be on your desk for the fix.
Correct. Start from the method and walk outward, keeping every page you read.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think an Explore subagent is always the tidy way to explore. It is right when the main session needs only conclusions. Here the engineer will write the fix in this session and wants the callers' code in view. A subagent's reads stay in its own context, so the main session gets only a summary.
deep.diagram:
Grep 'apply_regional_discount' -> matches -> Read each
  who calls those? -> Grep again -> Read
  (every read stays in this session for the fix)
deep.mapTitle: How should Claude explore code for this task?

head: Situation
Best approach
Why
rows: Known starting point, code needed for the fix
Grep, Read the hits, trace outward
Builds the picture step by step in this session
Only a conclusion needed, discovery is verbose
Keeps noisy output out of the main context
Looking for files by name or type
Small, unfamiliar folder to learn fully
Fine when the whole set is small
Long investigation that may lose its place
Keeps key facts across context limits

evidence.quote: the stack trace ends in one method, apply_regional_discount
evidence.means: There is a known starting point, which is exactly what Grep searches for by content.

evidence.quote: The engineer needs every path in the app that calls it
evidence.means: Every caller, wherever it lives. Guessing from file names ([[0]]) misses some.

evidence.quote: In this same session they will then write the fix, with the callers' real code in front of Claude
evidence.means: The decider. A subagent summary ([[2]]) leaves the code behind. [[3]] reads it into this session.

evidence.quote: billing code is spread across many folders
evidence.means: Reading everything first ([[1]]) fills the context with files that don't matter.

deep.rule: Known starting point → Grep for it, Read the hits, trace outward. Use a subagent only when a summary is enough.

guide.obj: 2.5 Select and apply built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob)
guide.quote: Build understanding incrementally: Grep entry points → Read to follow imports/trace flows (not read-all-upfront)

questions.question: The team is adding a Sentry MCP server so Claude can read production errors. Sentry gives each person their own token, and its audit log credits every action to the token's owner. Security wants no credential stored in the repository. New joiners should get the server as soon as they clone. How should the server be set up?

options.t: Each person adds the server to their own ~/.claude.json, with their personal token inline.
options.why: Works, but not shared. Each token stays personal and out of git, but joiners don't get the server on clone and must set it up by hand.

options.t: Commit the entry to .mcp.json, reading the token from ${SENTRY_TOKEN} in each shell.
options.why: Best. The entry is shared on clone, the file holds no secret, and each person's own token keeps the audit trail personal.

options.t: Commit the entry to .mcp.json, reading one shared team token from an environment variable.
options.why: Works, but every action is credited to one shared token, so the audit log can no longer say who did what.

options.t: Commit .mcp.json with an empty token field, and have each person paste in their own token.
options.why: Works, but only usually. A pasted token sits in a tracked file, and one careless commit puts it in the repository.

questions.decider: New joiners should get the server as soon as they clone.
questions.explanation: Shared MCP servers go in the project's .mcp.json, with secrets supplied by environment-variable expansion such as ${SENTRY_TOKEN}. User-level ~/.claude.json is for personal or experimental servers.

eli5.question: A shared tool needs a personal key for each person, and no keys may sit in the shared code. The clue: New joiners should get the server as soon as they clone, and the audit wants each action tied to a person.
eli5.answer: Think of an office door. The lock (the server entry) is the same for everyone and comes with the building. Each person carries their own key card (their token), and the log records whose card opened the door. In Claude Code the shared lock is .mcp.json in the repo, and ${SENTRY_TOKEN} tells it to read each person's own key from their shell. Rule: shared server in .mcp.json, secret through an environment variable.
options: Everyone fits their own lock at home. Keys stay private, but new people arrive to find no lock at all.
Correct. One shared lock, each person's own key card, and no key left in the building.
One shared card opens the door, but the log can no longer say who came in.
A blank slot for the key works until someone tapes their key into it and the copy gets shared.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a personal token means a personal config. The token is personal, but the server is shared. Claude Code splits the two: the server entry is committed in .mcp.json, and the token is filled in from each person's environment with ${VAR} expansion.
deep.mapTitle: Where does this MCP setting belong?

head: What you need
Where it goes
Why
rows: A server only you are trying out
Each action tied to a person
A shared token hides who acted

evidence.quote: Sentry gives each person their own token, and its audit log credits every action to the token's owner
evidence.means: Each person must use their own token. One team token ([[2]]) blurs the audit.

evidence.quote: Security wants no credential stored in the repository
evidence.means: The committed file may name a variable, not hold a value. A token pasted into a tracked file ([[3]]) is one commit away from breaking this.

evidence.quote: New joiners should get the server as soon as they clone
evidence.means: The decider. The entry must be in the repo, which rules out ~/.claude.json ([[0]]). [[1]] meets all three needs.

deep.rule: Shared server → .mcp.json in the repo. Secret → ${VAR} from each person's environment.

guide.obj: 2.4 Integrate MCP servers into Claude Code and agent workflows
guide.quote: Env var expansion in .mcp.json (e.g., ${GITHUB_TOKEN}) — no committed secrets

questions.question: Twenty minutes into a session, an engineer adds a Sentry server to the project's .mcp.json. They ask Claude for the latest events in an error group. Claude says none of its tools reach Sentry and offers to call Sentry's API with curl. The same entry works on a teammate's machine, and the engineer's token is set in their shell. What should the engineer do?

options.t: Exit, then start Claude Code again with --resume on this session, and ask once more.
options.why: Best. Claude Code finds MCP servers and their tools when it connects. A restart connects to the new server, and --resume keeps the work so far.

options.t: Expand the Sentry tools' descriptions, and ask Claude to prefer them over Bash and curl.
options.why: Works, but for a different problem. Better descriptions help Claude choose a tool it has. Here the tools were never loaded.

options.t: Accept Claude's offer, and let it fetch the events with curl through Bash for now.
options.why: Works, but a workaround. Claude gets the events this time, but the Sentry tools stay missing for the rest of the session.

options.t: Open a new terminal, start a fresh session there, and ask about the error group again.
options.why: Works, but loses the work. A new session connects to the server, but the findings so far stay behind in the old one.

questions.decider: Twenty minutes into a session, an engineer adds a Sentry server to the project's .mcp.json.
questions.explanation: Claude Code discovers MCP servers and their tools at connection time, so a server added mid-session needs a reconnect. Tell 'tool missing' apart from 'tool present but not chosen'.

eli5.question: Claude can't see a tool that was added while it was running. The clue: Twenty minutes into a session, an engineer adds a Sentry server. The entry itself is fine; it works elsewhere.
eli5.answer: Think of a TV that scans for channels only when you switch it on. Add a new channel while it is on, and it won't appear until you switch off and on again. Claude Code finds MCP tools when it connects (at connection time). Restarting with --resume rescans and keeps your place in the show. Rule: tool missing after a mid-session config change → reconnect. Tool present but not chosen → fix its description.
options: Correct. Switch off and on to rescan, and pick up where you left off.
A better channel guide helps you choose among channels you have. This channel isn't in the list yet.
Watching on your phone gets you tonight's show, but the TV still lacks the channel.
A second TV scans fresh, but you lose your place in what you were watching.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think Claude ignored the Sentry tools, so their descriptions need work. But Claude says no tool reaches Sentry: the tools are not there at all. Claude Code discovers MCP servers and their tools when it connects. A server added mid-session appears only after a reconnect.
deep.diagram:
start -> connect to servers in config -> tools loaded
add Sentry to .mcp.json    -> no new tools yet
restart with --resume      -> connect again -> Sentry
deep.mapTitle: Is the tool missing, or present but not chosen?

head: What you see
Cause
Fix
rows: Restart, with --resume to keep the work
Tools loaded, but Claude picks Bash or Grep
Works for a teammate, fails after a fresh start
Set the variable in your shell
Too many tools, wrong one chosen

evidence.quote: Twenty minutes into a session, an engineer adds a Sentry server to the project's .mcp.json
evidence.means: The decider. The server was added after the session had connected.

evidence.quote: Claude says none of its tools reach Sentry
evidence.means: The tools are missing, not ignored. Better descriptions ([[1]]) fix a different problem.

evidence.quote: The same entry works on a teammate's machine, and the engineer's token is set in their shell
evidence.means: The config and the token are fine. Only the connection is stale.

evidence.quote: What should the engineer do?
evidence.means: Reconnect and keep the work: [[0]]. curl ([[2]]) works around it; a fresh session ([[3]]) leaves the findings behind.

deep.rule: Tool missing after adding a server mid-session → reconnect. MCP tools are discovered at connection time.

guide.obj: 2.4 Integrate MCP servers into Claude Code and agent workflows
guide.quote: All configured MCP servers' tools discovered at connection time, available simultaneously

questions.question: A long pricing data file holds rate blocks for each region. The same eight-line default block appears four times, and the lines around each copy are identical too. The blocks are told apart only by their order in the file. Claude must change one rate in the third copy. Its Edit failed because the match text appears in all four places. What should Claude do next?

options.t: Run Edit with replace-all on the rate line, then change the other three copies back.
options.why: Works, but the wrong action first. It changes three copies that should stay, then needs three more edits to undo them, each as ambiguous as the first.

options.t: Read the whole file, then Write it back with the one rate changed in the third copy.
options.why: Best. With no unique text to match, Edit can't target one copy. Read plus Write is the fallback, and a diff review shows the single change.

options.t: Change the rate with sed through Bash, anchored on that copy's current line number.
options.why: Works, but fragile. A line number goes stale with any change above it, and the change skips any check that the line is the right one.

options.t: Add a comment naming the region above each copy, then Edit using that comment as the match.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt, and the first step hits the same problem. Adding four comments needs unique anchors too, all to make one edit possible.

questions.decider: The blocks are told apart only by their order in the file.
questions.explanation: Edit makes a targeted change by unique text match. When the match is not unique and no unique anchor exists, fall back to Read plus Write.

eli5.question: Claude must change one of four identical copies, and nothing nearby tells them apart. The clue: The blocks are told apart only by their order in the file.
eli5.answer: Think of a form with four identical boxes, and you must correct the third one. Saying 'change the box that reads Default rate' fails, because four boxes read that. With nothing unique to point at, you take the whole form, fix the third box, and hand back the whole form. In Claude Code that is Read the file, then Write it back with the one change. Rule: Edit match not unique and no unique text to anchor on → Read plus Write.
options: Correcting all four boxes and then undoing three is more work, and each undo has the same problem.
Correct. Take the whole form, fix the third box, hand it back.
'Change line 212' works until someone adds a line above it.
Labelling every box first would help, but labelling them runs into the same problem and is a big job for one fix.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think Edit can always be made to work with a cleverer match or a few prep steps. Edit needs match text that appears exactly once. Here the copies and the lines around them are identical, so no such text exists. The exam guide's answer is the fallback: Read the file and Write it back with the change.
deep.diagram:
Edit match: default block -> 4 places -> fails
no unique text near copy 3 -> Read file
  -> change rate in copy 3 -> Write file -> diff

head: Situation
Tool
Why
rows: One small change, match text unique
Edit match not unique, but unique text sits nearby
Edit match not unique, nothing nearby is unique
Every copy should change the same way

evidence.quote: the lines around each copy are identical too
evidence.means: Widening the match won't help: there is no unique text near the copy.

evidence.quote: The blocks are told apart only by their order in the file
evidence.means: The decider. Edit matches text, not position, so it can't pick the third copy. [[1]] is the fallback.

evidence.quote: Claude must change one rate in the third copy
evidence.means: Only one copy should change. Replace-all ([[0]]) changes four and needs undoing.

evidence.quote: Its Edit failed because the match text appears in all four places
evidence.means: The guide's case: Edit failed on a non-unique match. Line numbers ([[2]]) are fragile, and adding comments ([[3]]) hits the same problem first.

deep.rule: Edit fails on a non-unique match and no unique text exists → Read plus Write.

guide.obj: 2.5 Select and apply built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob)
guide.quote: When Edit fails on non-unique match → Read + Write fallback

questions.question: For error spikes, the engineer gives Claude a fixed plan: read the stack trace, the failing method and its callers, check the deploy diff, then propose a fix. Last time the method was fine. The bad value came from an upstream API client after another team's change. Claude still finished the plan and proposed a guard in the method. How should such investigations be run?

options.t: Hand each step of the plan to its own subagent, and have a coordinator merge the results.
options.why: Works, but the steps are still fixed. Subagents split the work, but none of them can follow a lead the plan didn't foresee.

options.t: Begin in plan mode, and have Claude write the full step list before it reads any code.
options.why: Works, but the list is fixed before any evidence. Plan mode suits designing a change, not an investigation whose next step depends on findings.

options.t: Keep the fixed plan, and add steps for upstream API clients and other teams' recent changes.
options.why: Works, but only for causes you foresaw. The next surprise will sit somewhere the longer list doesn't cover.

options.t: Give Claude the goal and the evidence so far, and let it pick each next step as it goes.
options.why: Best. When the method proves fine, Claude can turn upstream at once instead of finishing steps that no longer fit.

questions.decider: Last time the method was fine.
questions.explanation: Fixed sequential pipelines suit predictable work. Open-ended investigations need adaptive decomposition, where each next step comes from what the last one found.

eli5.question: Claude followed a checklist even after the evidence pointed elsewhere. The clue: Last time the method was fine, yet the plan carried on as if it weren't.
eli5.answer: Think of a doctor with a fixed checklist: check the knee, x-ray the knee, operate on the knee. If the knee is fine and the pain comes from the back, the checklist still ends in knee surgery. A good doctor picks each next test from the last result. For Claude, give the goal and the evidence, and let it choose each next step (adaptive investigation). Rule: steps known in advance → fixed plan. Next step depends on findings → let Claude adapt.
options: Four doctors each doing one knee step still all look at the knee.
Writing a fuller checklist before seeing the patient is still a checklist written blind.
Adding a back check helps this time, but the next pain may come from somewhere else again.
Correct. Each test is chosen from the last result.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the plan just missed a step, so a longer plan will fix it. The real fault is that the steps were fixed before anything was found. An investigation is open-ended: each next step depends on what the last one showed. That calls for adaptive decomposition, not a better fixed list.
deep.diagram:
fixed:    trace -> method -> callers -> diff -> fix
          (method fine, plan carries on)
adaptive: trace -> method fine -> look upstream -> ...

head: Kind of work
Structure
Why
rows: Goal plus evidence; Claude picks each next step
Same steps every time, such as per-file review
Known extra causes to check every time
Independent parts to cover in parallel
Splits the work, not the choice of steps

evidence.quote: the engineer gives Claude a fixed plan
evidence.means: The steps are set before anything is read.

evidence.quote: Last time the method was fine
evidence.means: The decider. The findings changed direction, but the plan could not.

evidence.quote: The bad value came from an upstream API client after another team's change
evidence.means: The cause sat outside every step. Adding this step ([[2]]) covers this case, not the next one.

evidence.quote: Claude still finished the plan and proposed a guard in the method
evidence.means: The plan overrode the evidence. Only [[3]] lets the evidence choose the next step; [[0]] and [[1]] still fix the steps up front.

deep.rule: Open-ended investigation → give the goal and let Claude adapt each step. Predictable work → fixed sequence.

guide.obj: 1.6 Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
guide.quote: Adaptive investigation plans generate subtasks from what's discovered

questions.question: It is late in a long incident session, and the context window is nearly full. The engineer spawns an Explore subagent. Its prompt says: 'Investigate the issue we've been discussing and report the call paths involved.' It returns a broad tour of the serializer code. It never mentions the failing frame, the changed field or the other team's change. Which TWO changes would most improve the next attempt?

options.t: Write the failing frame, the changed field and the suspect serializer into its prompt.
options.why: Best. A subagent starts with none of the session's history, so the findings must be in its prompt.

options.t: Fork the session and do the mapping in the branch, which already holds the incident history.
options.why: Works, but the branch starts nearly full. It has the history, but little room is left for the mapping work.

options.t: Give the subagent the main session's full tool list, including the Sentry and Linear tools.
options.why: Works, but for a different problem. More tools don't tell the subagent what to look for.

options.t: Say what to send back: each path from entry point to serializer, with its files and lines.
options.why: Best. A stated deliverable tells the subagent what done looks like, instead of leaving it to tour.

questions.decider: Its prompt says: 'Investigate the issue we've been discussing and report the call paths involved.'
questions.explanation: Subagents start with isolated context: pass the relevant findings explicitly and state the deliverable and its quality criteria. Forking carries the history along, which helps only when there is room for it.

eli5.question: A helper was sent off with 'look into what we discussed', but the helper wasn't in the discussion. The clue: Investigate the issue we've been discussing.
eli5.answer: Think of sending a courier with a note that says 'fetch the thing we talked about'. The courier wasn't there, so they bring back a bit of everything. Fix the note two ways: say what you already know (the frame, the field, the suspect), and say exactly what to bring back (each path, with files and lines). A subagent starts with an empty memory (isolated context); only its prompt tells it anything. Rule: a subagent knows only its prompt, so give it the findings and the deliverable.
options: Correct. Tell the courier what you already know.
Cloning yourself works, but your clone arrives with a full desk and no room to work.
A bigger toolbox doesn't tell the courier what to fetch.
Correct. Tell the courier exactly what to bring back.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a subagent knows what the session knows. It doesn't. A subagent starts with isolated context: no history, only its prompt. 'The issue we've been discussing' points at nothing. The fix is to put the findings in the prompt and to state the deliverable.
deep.diagram:
main session (nearly full): frame, field, suspect
   | prompt: 'the issue we've been discussing'
   v
subagent: empty context -> broad tour
deep.mapTitle: What does the subagent need from you?

head: Situation
Best move
Why
rows: State the deliverable and when it is complete
Try another approach from a shared baseline, with room to spare
The branch keeps the shared history
Delegate with a short, explicit prompt
Keeps verbose work out of the main session
Add that tool to its list

evidence.quote: the context window is nearly full
evidence.means: A fork ([[1]]) would start with that same nearly full history.

evidence.quote: Investigate the issue we've been discussing and report the call paths involved
evidence.means: The decider. The subagent wasn't there, and 'report the call paths' doesn't say what complete looks like.

evidence.quote: It returns a broad tour of the serializer code
evidence.means: No stated deliverable, so it toured. Name the output: [[3]].

evidence.quote: It never mentions the failing frame, the changed field or the other team's change
evidence.means: It lacked the findings, not the tools ([[2]]). Give it the findings: [[0]].

deep.rule: A subagent knows only its prompt: pass the findings and state the deliverable.

guide.obj: 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
guide.quote: Subagent context must be provided explicitly in the prompt (no automatic inheritance / shared memory)

questions.question: Early in a session, Claude reads the pricing service file. The engineer then changes apply_regional_discount in their own editor and saves. Later, Claude explains that method by quoting the old version, line numbers and all. The session is still short, and the work so far is useful. What should the engineer do?

options.t: Tell Claude the file changed, and ask it to Read the file again before going on.
options.why: Best. The old Read result stays in the history Claude sees each turn. A fresh Read puts the current version there.

options.t: Run /compact, then ask Claude to explain the method again from its summary.
options.why: Works, but the summary still comes from the old read. It shrinks the history without bringing in the new code.

options.t: Start a new session with a summary of the findings, and have it read the file fresh.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. It drops a short, useful session to fix one stale read that a single Read fixes.

options.t: Add a note to CLAUDE.md asking Claude to re-read files before it quotes them.
options.why: Works, but only usually, and it costs a re-read every time. Claude still can't know the file changed unless told.

questions.decider: The engineer then changes apply_regional_discount in their own editor and saves.
questions.explanation: Tool results are appended to the conversation history, and Claude reasons over them on every later turn. When a file changes outside the session, tell Claude and have it read again.

eli5.question: Claude is quoting a file from memory after someone changed it. The clue: changes apply_regional_discount in their own editor, outside Claude's view.
eli5.answer: Think of a photo you took of a whiteboard. Someone rubs out a line and writes a new one, but your photo still shows the old line. Claude's earlier Read is that photo: it sits in the conversation history (tool results), and Claude uses it every turn. Tell Claude the board changed and take a new photo (Read again). Rule: file changed outside Claude → tell it, and have it read again.
options: Correct. Say the board changed, and take a new photo.
Shrinking your photo album still leaves the old photo, just smaller.
A new notebook with a fresh photo works, but you throw away good notes to fix one picture.
A standing reminder to re-photograph everything is slow, and Claude still doesn't know which board changed.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think Claude has a memory that should refresh when files change. There is no separate memory. The earlier Read result is part of the conversation history, sent with every turn. It stays as it was until Claude is told about the change or reads the file again.
deep.diagram:
turn 3: Read pricing file -> result added to history
(engineer edits the file in their own editor)
turn 9: Claude reasons over history -> old version
deep.mapTitle: Why is Claude working from old information?

head: What you see
Cause
Fix
rows: Claude quotes a file changed outside the session
Old Read result in the history
Long session, answers drift to generic patterns
Resuming days later after much code changed
New session with a structured summary
Resume and tell Claude what changed

evidence.quote: Early in a session, Claude reads the pricing service file
evidence.means: That Read result is now part of the history Claude sees each turn.

evidence.quote: The engineer then changes apply_regional_discount in their own editor and saves
evidence.means: The decider. The change happened outside the session, so nothing tells Claude. [[0]] tells it and reads again.

evidence.quote: The session is still short, and the work so far is useful
evidence.means: Nothing is degrading. /compact ([[1]]) and a new session ([[2]]) solve problems this session doesn't have.

deep.rule: Tool results live in the conversation history. When a file changes outside the session, tell Claude and read again.

guide.obj: 1.1 Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
guide.quote: Tool results are appended to conversation history so the model reasons about the next action

questions.question: The Sentry MCP server brings read tools for errors and stack traces. It also brings tools that resolve, assign and delete issues. Last week Claude resolved an issue it judged fixed, without asking anyone. Team policy says issue state changes only in Sentry's own interface, where each change is credited to a person. Which control best fits the policy?

options.t: A PreToolUse hook that asks the engineer to approve any Sentry call that changes issue state.
options.why: Works, but it still lets a session change issue state after one click. The policy says those changes happen only in Sentry.

options.t: A rule in the project CLAUDE.md saying issue state changes only in Sentry's interface.
options.why: Works, but only usually. An instruction is followed most of the time, and the tools stay within reach.

options.t: Deny the Sentry tools that resolve, assign or delete issues in the committed project settings.
options.why: Best. The tools that change issue state are gone for everyone on clone, and the read tools stay.

options.t: Disconnect the server, and have engineers paste stack traces into the conversation.
options.why: Works, but it removes the read tools too, which the team uses for every incident.

questions.decider: Team policy says issue state changes only in Sentry's own interface, where each change is credited to a person.
questions.explanation: Give an agent only the tools its role needs. When an action must not happen from the agent at all, remove access to it; approval steps fit actions that are allowed with a sign-off.

eli5.question: Claude has buttons it is never supposed to press. The clue: issue state changes only in Sentry's own interface. Not 'with approval'; only there.
eli5.answer: Think of a shop assistant who may look at the stock but must never change prices. You don't ask them to check with you each time, and you don't just put up a sign. You give them a badge that doesn't open the pricing room. In Claude Code that badge is a deny list in the committed project settings: the read tools stay, the state-changing tools are gone. Rule: an action that must never happen from the agent → take the tool away. Allowed with sign-off → approval hook.
options: Asking you before each price change still lets prices change from the shop floor.
A sign saying 'don't change prices' is usually obeyed, not always.
Correct. The badge opens the stockroom, not the pricing room.
Sending the assistant home stops price changes, but nobody can check the stock either.
